title: AI Will Improve Your Workplace—So Long As You Have a Learning Culture
author: Melissa Muth Martinez
summary: Melissa Muth Martinez argues that whether AI makes an organization better depends on the learning culture it sits inside. If learning is treated as information transfer, AI simply speeds up the same mistakes and capability stays fragile. Drawing on Bransford and Ericsson, she holds that capability comes from application across contexts, deliberate practice and feedback, which AI can accelerate only if it is used alongside those mechanics. She illustrates the contrast with four scenarios: performance reviews, change management, cross-department collaboration and onboarding. Her practical starting move is small: when someone uses AI for a quick answer, also have them generate questions that provoke reflection and collaboration.
points: AI amplifies whatever learning foundation exists; it does not repair a broken one.
Treating learning as information transfer makes AI a faster way to produce polished but brittle performance.
Capability still requires repetition, struggle in new contexts and feedback loops, regardless of AI.
In the manager-preparing-for-a-hard-conversation example, AI used for reflection and scenario exploration builds judgment while AI-drafted scripts do not.
A low-stakes first step is pairing every AI answer with questions like what assumptions am I making here.
quotes: If your organization treats learning as little more than information overload and transfer, AI may help people generate faster answers, but long-term capability will be fragile. Conversely, if you design your systems around learning—and more specifically, its principles of judgment, reflection, and shared understanding—AI becomes a tool for building long-term, transformative capability.
When organizations implement AI with their minds heavily fixed on efficiency and immediacy, they’re essentially digitizing the same mistakes, but simply doing so at a pace that looks more impressive.

This matters because, even with AI, the core mechanics of how we learn haven’t changed. We still need repetition, we still need to struggle with application in new contexts, and we still need feedback loops that help us refine our thinking. AI can accelerate some of this, but only if we employ it alongside these cognitive realities rather than around the allure of speed.

Performance Reviews. Consider a manager preparing for a difficult performance conversation. In organizations oriented around speed, the manager might ask AI to draft feedback or talking points for them. At first glance, the conversation sounds polished, but when the employee reacts with a heightened level of emotion or raises unexpected concerns, the manager struggles. While they have a nice script, their judgment is lacking.

In each of the above cases, the differentiator isn't AI, but how it's used within the organization's learning infrastructure. AI will serve as an amplifier to whatever foundation already exists—either building shared understanding, judgment, and coordination, or simply accelerating output in the short-term without strengthening capability in the long-term. The first might look prettier, but it’s also more fragile.

I don’t believe AI will fix a broken workplace. On it’s own, it can’t create these kinds of outcomes. But a strong, learning-centric culture combined with AI has the power to do that and more, turning fragility into transformative capability.
